Anyone can wire up an LLM and call it an "agent." Shipping one that survives real users is a different discipline entirely. Here's the full path.

1. Discover
• Understand the business problem, identify target users, and set success criteria for accuracy and latency.
• Map risks like bias and privacy before a single line of code.
• Skip this and you'll build something impressive that nobody actually needed.

2. Design
• Set rules and guardrails, outline the decision flow, and define the agent loop (ReAct, Plan-Execute).
• Choose the agent type that fits the problem, not the hype.
• Architecture decided here is what you'll either thank or curse yourself for later.

3. Connect
• Integrate APIs and tools, add short-term memory via the context window, and long-term memory using vector DBs like Weaviate.
• Enable context awareness so the agent remembers what matters.
• Memory is what separates a chatbot from an agent that can actually get work done.

4. Prompt
• Structure inputs with prompt templates, define tools via function calling, and add few-shot examples.
• Write and refine prompts deliberately, not by guesswork.
• Prompting is engineering, not magic words, and it's where most agents quietly fail.

5. Ground
• Chunk reference data, embed with vectors, build a search pipeline (keyword + semantic), and connect a retrieval layer using RAG.
• Give the agent access to real, current knowledge.
• Grounding is your best defense against the model confidently making things up.

6. Test
• Refine with feedback, simulate edge cases, and evaluate for correctness and hallucination.
• Run tests with proper evaluation frameworks.
• "It worked in my demo" is not a testing strategy.

7. Deploy
• Launch with FastAPI or Docker, monitor usage with LangSmith, and log failures and tool traces.
• Update iteratively using Git and CI/CD.
• Deployment is the start of the work, not the finish line.

Great AI agents aren't prompted into existence. They're engineered, stage by stage.
